lines.text: כן 475 כנו
of relative conjunctions Lehrg. p. 636.
Ps. 45, 3 thou art fairer than the children
of men... עַל־כֵּן בֵּרַכְךָ אֱלֹהִים because
that God hath blessed thee for ever. Ps.
e) עַד־כֵּן lit. until so, i. e. until now, as
yet, hitherto, Neh. 2, 16. Here כֵּן refers
to time as in Syriac; see note above.
f) כְּמוֹ־כֵן like this, in like manner,
Is. 51, 6; comp. Engl. such-like. Sept.
ὥσπερ ταῦτα, Vulg. sicut hæc; and so
all the ancient versions. But see in כֵּן
III.—R.
II. כֵּן m. (r. כָּנַן I) c. suff. כַּנִּי, כַּנּוֹ.
1. a stand, base, pedestal; 1 K. 7, 31
מַעֲשֵׂה־כֵן in the manner of a base, like a
pedestal. Spec. of the base or foot of
the laver in the court of the temple, Ex.
base or socket of a ship’s mast, Is. 33, 23;
called in Greek μεσόδμη Od. 15. 290,
ἱστοδόκη Il. 1. 494, ἱστοπέδη Od. 12. 51.
2. a stand, station, place, Gen. 40, 13.
41. 13. Dan. 11, 20 וְעָמַד עַל כַּנּוֹ and there
shall rise up in his place, in his stead. v.
21. 38. So v. 7 וְעָמַד מִנֵּצֶר שָׁרָשֶׁיהָ כַּנּוֹ
and out of a shoot of her roots (one) shall
rise up in his place, pr. stand in his place.
Sept. and Vulg. render כַּנּוֹ by φυτόν αὐ-
τοῦ, plantatio ejus, taking it in the nom.
case; see in כִּנָּה.
III. כֵּן m. (r. כָּנַן II) a gnat, in Sing.
once Is. 51, 6 כְּמוֹ־כֵן like gnats. Sept.
frigidly ὥσπερ ταῦτα, Vulg. sicut hæc;
see in כֵּן I. B. f. above.
Sept. σκνῖφες, Vulg. sciniphes, a species
of small gnats, very troublesome from
their sting, and abounding in the marshy
regions of Egypt; culex reptans Linn.
culex molestus Forsk. See Hdot. 1. 95.
Philo de vita Mosis T. II. p. 97 ed. Man-
gey. Other ancient and modern testi-
monies are collected in Bochart Hieroz.
II. p. 572. Oedmann’s Verm. Sammll.
aus der Naturkunde, Fasc. I. c. 6.—The
Hebrew intpp. and Josephus (Ant. 2. 14.
3) with little probability explain it by
lice; and the Talmudists also use the
sing. כִּנָּם for a louse. Comp. כִּנָּם.
כֵּן Chald. i. q. Heb. so, thus, but re-
ferring always to what follows, where
the Hebrews use not כֵּן, but כֹּה; so
* כָּנָה in Kal not used, Arab. كنى
I, II, IV, to call a person or thing by
another and more honourable name or
title, to deck with a title; see Tauriz.
ad Hamas. Schult. p. 320. Teblebi ad
Harir. Schult. II. 57. Chald. to address
one by his proper title. The primary
idea is perh. to cover, comp. גָּנַן.—In
Heb. only
Piel fut. יְכַנֶּה 1. to address in a
soothing manner, to speak kindly to any
one. Is. 44, 5 וּבְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֶּה and
soothingly names the name of Israel.
45, 4 אֲכַנְּךָ וְלֹא יְדַעְתָּנִי I called thee
kindly, though thou hast not known me.
2. to flatter, Job 32, 21. 22.
Deriv. subst. כְּנָת.
כַּנָּה f. (r. כָּנַן I) a plant, shoot, as be-
ing set, placed; comp. נָצַב, שָׁתַל. Ps.
80, 16 וְכַנָּה אֲשֶׁר נָטְעָה יְמִינֶךָ and (visit,
protect) the plant which thy right hand
hath planted. The ancient intpp. as-
sumed also the masc. כֵּן in the same
sense Dan. 11, 7; see in כֵּן II. 2.—Others
here make כַּנָּה imper. Kal with He pa-
ragog. from r. כָּנַן in a signif. to cover, to
protect; of which however there is no
other trace.
כַּנֵּה ἅπ. λεγόμ. Ez. 27, 23, Canneh, pr.
n. of a city, prob. Ctesiphon, i. q. כַּלְנֵה
which also is read in one of De Rossi’s
Mss. Comp. יִקַּח for וְיִלְקַח; see more
in כַּלְנֶה.
כִּנְרוֹת see כִּנֶּרֶת.
כִּנּוֹר m. (r. כָּנַר) plur. כִּנֹּרוֹת 1 K. 10,
12, c. suff. כִּנֹּרוֹתֵינוּ Ps. 137, 2, once
כִּנּוֹרַיִךְ Ez. 26, 13; Gr. κινύρα, κιννύρα,
a species of harp or lyre, Lat. cithara,
[whence the modern word guitar,] a
stringed instrument of music, celebrated
for David’s skill in playing upon it, and
employed both in sacred and profane
music, in rejoicing and in mourning,
Job 30, 31; usually as an accompaniment
22. al. Josephus relates, Ant. 7. 12. 3,
that the κινύρα had ten strings, and was
struck with a plectrum; but this is con-
trary to the words in 1 Sam. 16, 23. 18,
10. 19, 9, from which it appears that this
instrument was played with the fingers.

line_status.note: The final (leftmost) letter of the right-hand word is a narrow vertical stroke with no broad head extending left — a vav, not a resh; so כנו, not כנר.

The root in parentheses is printed as three letters כָּנַן (kaph–nun–final nun, with qamets and pathach), not כּוּן; the rest of the line (כֵּן, suffixed forms כַּנִּי then כַּנּוֹ) is identical in both readings and matches the print.
Final word: the ḥolem is printed over the vav (כַּנּוֹ, ḥolem male), not over the nun as in B's נֹּו; the nun carries only dagesh. A matches the print.

Hebrew: the holam dot sits over the vav (holam male), so the correct encoding is nun+dagesh, vav, holam (כַּנּוֹ) as in A, not B's holam-before-vav (כַּנֹּו). Greek: the accent on φυτόν is printed as an acute (´), as in B, not A's grave (φυτὸν). Each reading has one error, so neither matches the print.

The decisive difference is the dagesh in the second kaf: the printed כֵן after the maqqef shows only tsere beneath the kaf with no dot inside it (contrast the clearly dotted first kaf כְּ), so Reading A's undageshed כֵן matches the print.

After "6" the print shows a baseline period with only a detached speck beneath it, not the continuous comma tail seen after "5"; so "6. 2." (Reading A), not "6, 2." (Reading B). "4 11" is indeed printed without a comma.

Final letter is ת (tav, with its distinct left foot), not ה; the mark under the kaf is a vertical two-dot shewa, not a single hiriq dot. Kaf carries dagesh lene, nun has qamets. Reading B matches; Reading A's כִּנָּה is wrong in final letter and first vowel.

Both Hebrew words print qamets under the first letter (T-shaped mark under nun and under shin) and patach (flat stroke) under the second (tsade, tav) — נָצַב, שָׁתַל, matching Reading A; Reading B's sheva + qamets / sheva + hireq is not what is printed. Shin dot is at top right in both readings and in print.
Under the nun two dots are printed side by side (tsere), not a single segol cluster; the rest of the line is identical in both readings.
Under the nun of the final Hebrew word two dots are printed side by side (tsere), not three (segol); the rest of the line is identical in both readings.

The second Hebrew word is printed with five letters: vav (sheva) + yod (hireq) + lamed (sheva) + qof (patah) + chet, i.e. וְיִלְקַח. Reading A drops the yod and mis-points (וְלֶקַח); Reading B drops the initial vav (יִלְקַח). The first word יִקַּח (with dagesh in qof) is correct in both.

The first syllable is printed defectively: the nun carries dagesh and a holem dot directly above it, followed immediately by resh — there is no vav between nun and resh (matching the defective plural כִּנֹּרוֹת in the line above). Only the second holem is written with vav (וֹ).
